files.lesson.md: --- order: 14 unit: chance node: [AC9M8P03 n1, AC9M8P03 n2] uses: [AC9M8P02 n1, AC9M7P02 n2] title: Simulating compound events summary: "A computer can repeat a chance experiment thousands of times in a second. Run a simulation of two events, record the results in a frequency table, and compare the relative frequency with the probability from the sample space." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "In a board game you roll two dice every turn. Which total should you hope for, and how sure can you be? Rolling by hand would take all lesson; a simulation takes a second." connection: penalty-shootout # data/connections/maths.yml (documentation only) app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8332 url: http://127.0.0.1:8332/index.html readySelector: "#gtrial" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: sim.yml#explain-pic, caption: "Two dice: a total of 8 is 5 of the 36 outcomes, P = 5/36 ≈ 0.14. A simulation's relative frequency should come close to this over many trials." } explainClip: query: { code: "@sim.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "A simulation" say: "Many trials, recorded in a table, then compared with the probability." clip: - caption: { text: "Event A: a total of 8, P(A) = 5/36 ≈ 0.14. Run 10 trials.", say: "A total of eight has probability five out of thirty-six. Ten trials first." } - click: Run 10 - wait: 1400 - caption: { text: "1000 more: the relative frequency settles near 0.14.", say: "A thousand more, and it settles near the probability." } - click: Run 1000 - expect: { selector: "#gtrial", contains: "Trial 1010" } - wait: 2000 --- A **simulation** uses random numbers to act out a chance experiment, many times and quickly. Each repeat is a **trial**. Record the results in a **frequency table**, then find the **relative frequency** of the event: how many times it happened ÷ the number of trials. The board is one digital tool. In a spreadsheet, `=RANDBETWEEN(1,6)` is one roll of a dice: a whole number from 1 to 6, each equally likely. ## Predict: the most common total ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to the most likely sum of two dice shows whether they think the sums 2 to 12 are equally likely." check: type: predict q: "Two dice are rolled 100 times and the totals recorded. Which total will probably come up most often?" options: ["12", "They will all come up about the same", "7"] actual: "7. More pairs make 7 (six of the 36) than any other total; 2 and 12 have just one pair each." ``` ## Run: 100 trials ```step stage: run insight: "Running 100 trials of two dice and reading the frequency table shows the middle totals come up most, as the grid predicts." try: { playground: board, starter: "sim.yml#run", height: 760 } check: { type: board, text: "Run at least 100 trials. Which total came up most in the table? Is the relative frequency of 7 close to P(7)? Compare with your prediction.", when: "u >= 100", explain: "7 usually comes up most, close to 1/6 of the time. In 100 trials it can be a little off: the next step looks at why." } ``` The table counts each total. The **Probability** column comes from the grid: the number of pairs with that total out of 36. ## Investigate: reading a simulation ```step stage: investigate insight: "Relative frequency is count ÷ trials; a short run can't show a probability is 0 (Ella); simulating two dice means adding two dice, not one random total." tasks: - check: type: number q: "In 200 simulated rolls of two dice, a total of 7 came up 31 times. What is its relative frequency?" answer: 0.155 tolerance: 0.0005 feedback: - ["31", "Divide by the number of trials."] explain: "31 ÷ 200 = 0.155, close to 1/6 ≈ 0.167." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#ella" text: "Ella runs a short simulation. Click the line where her conclusion goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: sim-too-few explain: "Line 3: in 20 rolls, a 1-in-36 event more often than not doesn't happen at all. P(12) = 1/36 from the grid; a short run can't show it is impossible." - check: type: question q: "In a spreadsheet, A2 and B2 each hold =RANDBETWEEN(1,6), one dice each. Which formula in C2 simulates the total of two dice?" options: ["=RANDBETWEEN(1,12)", "=A2+B2", "=RANDBETWEEN(2,12)", "=A2*B2"] answer: 1 feedback: ["A total of 1 is impossible, and the totals are not equally likely.", null, "That makes 2 to 12 equally likely, but a total of 7 is six times as likely as 12.", "That multiplies the dice."] explain: "Add the two dice. One random number from 2 to 12 would make every total equally likely, which two dice don't." ``` ### Relative frequency Here is the routine. ```worked \text{Event: total of 9};\ P = \tfrac{4}{36} \approx 0.11 :: Predict from the grid first. \text{Run } 500 \text{ trials: } 9 \text{ came up } 58 \text{ times} :: Simulate and record. 58 \div 500 = 0.116 :: Relative frequency. 0.116 \approx 0.11 :: Close: more trials would make it closer still. ``` ### Find the mistake Read Ella's working. How many times would you expect a 12 in 20 rolls? ### Two dice in a spreadsheet ## Modify: more trials, other events ```step stage: modify insight: "More trials bring the relative frequency close to the probability; a different compound event (coins) behaves the same; A and not A always share the trials." try: { playground: board, starter: "sim.yml#run", height: 760 } tasks: - starter: "sim.yml#run" check: { type: board, text: "Run 1000 trials or more of two dice. Is the relative frequency of 7 within 0.04 of P(7) now?", when: "u >= 1000 and e < 0.04", explain: "With 1000 trials the relative frequency is almost always within about 0.03 of 1/6." } - starter: "sim.yml#coins" check: { type: board, text: "Two coins: the board shows P(at least one head) = 3/4. Say why, using the four outcomes. Then run 1000 trials or more: does the relative frequency agree?", when: "u >= 1000 and e < 0.05", explain: "Only TT has no head, so 3 of the 4 outcomes: 3/4. The relative frequency settles near 0.75." } - check: type: question q: "In a simulation, A happened 380 times in 500 trials. How many times did not A happen?" options: ["500", "You can't tell", "120", "380"] answer: 2 feedback: ["That is every trial.", "Every trial is in A or not A.", null, "That is A."] explain: "500 − 380 = 120. Relative frequencies 0.76 and 0.24 add to 1, just like complementary probabilities." - check: type: number q: "Two dice are rolled 600 times. About how many times do you expect a total of 7?" answer: 100 tolerance: 0 explain: "1/6 × 600 = 100. A simulation will give a number near 100, not exactly." smaller: check: { type: number, q: "Look at the grid of two dice. How many of the 36 pairs make a total of 7?", answer: 6, tolerance: 0, feedback: [[1, "Count them all: (1, 6), (2, 5), and so on."]], explain: "(1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2), (6, 1): 6 of 36, which is 1/6. Now share that over 600 rolls." } ``` ### 1000 trials ### At least one head ### A and not A ### Expected count ## Practise: simulations ```step stage: practise insight: "Recording results in a frequency table and judging a simulation, mixed; trusting a short run is the planted slip; 'or' is the review." tasks: - check: type: trace text: "A simulation of two coins recorded these 20 trials: HT, HH, TT, TH, HH, HT, TT, HH, TH, HT, TT, HH, HT, TH, TT, HH, HT, TH, TT, HH. Fill in the frequency table." table: | | outcome | HH | HT | TH | TT | | count | [6] | [5] | [4] | [5] | explain: "Tally each outcome: 6 + 5 + 4 + 5 = 20 trials. The relative frequency of HH is 6 ÷ 20 = 0.3, near P(HH) = 0.25." - check: type: question q: "Two classes simulate a total of 7 on two dice. Class A: 9 times in 40 trials. Class B: 170 times in 1000. Which estimate is more reliable?" options: ["Class A: its relative frequency (0.225) is bigger", "They are equally good", "Neither: simulations don't work", "Class B"] answer: 3 feedback: ["Reliability comes from the number of trials.", "1000 trials beat 40.", "Large simulations give good estimates.", null] explain: "More trials: 0.17 from 1000 trials is far steadier than 0.225 from 40." - check: type: question q: "A simulated relative frequency is 0.31 and the probability from the sample space is 1/3. What should you say?" options: ["The probability is wrong", "The probability is really 0.31", "They agree well enough", "The simulation is broken"] answer: 2 feedback: ["1/3 comes from counting equally likely outcomes.", "A simulation estimates; the sample space gives the exact value.", null, "Some difference is normal."] explain: "They are close: the difference is chance. Relative frequency varies, and settles near the probability as the trials grow." - check: type: answer q: "Review: 30 students, 18 play netball, 10 play hockey, 4 play both. What is P(netball or hockey)?" answer: "24/30" feedback: - ["28/30", "The 4 with both are counted twice."] explain: "18 + 10 − 4 = 24, so 24/30 = 4/5." ``` ### A frequency table ### Which estimate ### Close enough ### Review: or ## Make: your own simulation ```step stage: make insight: "Choosing an event, predicting, simulating and describing the result is the whole cycle of a simulation." try: { playground: board, starter: "sim.yml#free", height: 760 } hint: ["Choose any event, such as 'the total is a prime number' or 'both dice are odd'.", "Work out P(A) from the grid before you press Run."] check: { type: board, text: "Choose your own event on two dice, work out its probability, then run at least 1000 trials.", when: "n >= 1 and u >= 1000", explain: "Your relative frequency should be close to your probability. If it isn't, check your count of outcomes." } ``` Describe your result in a sentence: the event, its probability, the relative frequency after your trials, and whether they agree. ## Make: on paper ```step stage: make insight: "Comparing a made-up shootout simulation with 0.8 to the fifth, with the reason for the comparison picked at the key step." check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A striker scores 4 penalties in 5. A simulation of 200 five-kick shootouts, each kick scoring with probability 0.8, had her score all five in 64 of them (made up). What is the relative frequency of 'all five'? Compare it with $0.8^5 \\approx 0.33$. Work it out on paper." steps: - ["$64 \\div 200 = 0.32$", "relative frequency = count ÷ trials"] - ["$0.8^5 \\approx 0.33$", "the theoretical chance: five scores in a row, 0.8 each time"] - ["0.32 is close to 0.33, so the simulation matches the 0.8 rate; 200 trials still vary a little", "compare the frequency with the probability"] picks: - step: 3 q: "What does comparing 0.32 with 0.33 tell you?" options: ["The simulation is close to the theory, and a small gap is what chance gives in 200 trials", "The simulation is wrong because 0.32 is not 0.33", "The simulation proves the chance is exactly 0.32"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "A small gap is normal for a limited number of trials.", "A simulation estimates the chance. It does not prove an exact value."] answer: "0.32" answerLabel: "Relative frequency" tolerance: 0.005 feedback: - ["64", "That is the count. Divide by the 200 shootouts."] - ["0.33", "That is the theoretical chance. The simulation's own relative frequency is 64 ÷ 200."] criteria: - "I divided the count by the 200 trials." - "I put the simulated and theoretical values side by side." - "I said what the gap means, with the number of trials in my sentence." explain: "64 ÷ 200 = 0.32, close to 0.8⁵ ≈ 0.33. A small gap is expected from 200 trials." ``` Do this one in your book or on paper, one step per line, before you type the number. **Also used in** - **Sport.** A striker who scores 4 in 5 might score all five in a shootout about a third of the time. Simulate it, then check. - **Games.** Designers simulate thousands of plays instead of playing them. - **Class work.** Choose an event on two dice, predict its probability, then test it. ```teacher summary: Students simulate two dice and two coins, record results in a frequency table, and compare relative frequencies with probabilities from the sample space (AC9M8P03, nodes 1 and 2). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 10 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 15 min goals: - I can run a simulation of two events and record the results in a frequency table. - I can find a relative frequency and compare it with the probability. - I can explain why more trials give a better estimate. struggle: "Trusting a short run. Ask: how many times would you expect it in this many trials? Then: is what happened surprising?" before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need the two-dice grid (Grids and tree diagrams), complements, and relative frequency and the law of large numbers (Year 7 Many trials). The one idea: a simulation is many quick trials; its relative frequency estimates the probability and gets closer as trials grow. The common mistake is concluding from a short run (Ella's mistake: no 12 in 20 rolls, so impossible). The board is one digital tool. Others for a class task: a spreadsheet (=RANDBETWEEN(1,6) in two columns, a sum column, COUNTIF for the frequency table, filled down 1000 rows), an online dice simulator, or a short Python program. Generative AI can write a simulation, but students should check its code and its frequency table against the grid: an AI may describe results it never ran. Wider: simulate something with no simple sample space, such as how many packets of cereal you buy to collect all 6 cards. running: - "Predict: ask how many pairs make 7, and how many make 12." - "Run: ask which totals are rare, and why." - "Investigate: ask how many 12s Ella should expect in 20 rolls." - "Modify: ask what happens to the gap between f and P as trials grow." - "Make: ask for the probability before the Run button." - "Paper: the shootout comparison is worked on paper; the page marks the relative frequency and the reason for comparing, then shows a model. Books out." stuck: - see: A student says the simulation is wrong because 7 came up 15 times in 100, not 17. ask: Would a real dice give exactly 17? fix: Simulations vary like real trials; more trials, closer results. - see: A student reports a count as a relative frequency. ask: Out of how many trials? fix: Relative frequency = count ÷ trials. - see: A student expects the sums 2 to 12 to be equally likely. ask: How many pairs in the grid make 2? Make 7? fix: "Count pairs: the middle totals have more." stretch: Build the two-dice simulation in a spreadsheet with 1000 rows and a frequency table. Does it agree with the board? support: A frequency table template for totals 2 to 12 with columns for count, relative frequency and probability. leads: > This covers AC9M8P03. Where it leads: statistics from samples (Year 8 Statistics), and independent events and simulations in Years 9 and 10. exit: q: A simulation gives a total of 8 on two dice 68 times in 500 trials. Find the relative frequency and compare it with the probability. a: "68 ÷ 500 = 0.136. P(8) = 5/36 ≈ 0.139: very close." explain: > A **simulation** repeats a chance experiment many times with random numbers. Record each result in a **frequency table**, then **relative frequency** = count ÷ trials. Compare it with the **probability** from the sample space. A short run can be well off; over many trials the relative frequency settles close to the probability. A simulation estimates; the grid gives the exact value. ```
files.sim.yml:
# Simulated trials of two events for "Simulating compound events". Run adds trials; the table counts each result.

# region: run
widget: events
first: dice
second: dice
show: sum
event: s = 7
trials: on
# endregion

# region: explain
widget: events
first: dice
second: dice
show: sum
event: s = 8
trials: on
seed: 5
# endregion

# region: explain-pic
widget: events
first: dice
second: dice
show: sum
event: s = 8
# endregion

# region: coins
widget: events
first: coin
second: coin
names: First coin, Second coin
event: a = H or b = H
choose: off
trials: on
# endregion

# region: free
widget: events
first: dice
second: dice
show: sum
trials: on
# endregion

# Ella's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: ella
Ella uses an app to roll two dice 20 times.
A sum of 12 never comes up in her 20 rolls.
So the probability of a sum of 12 is 0.
